Teacher: Sofía Vilá
The Optimizing Effect of Fungi Lion’s Mane (Hericium rinaceus) for Growing Radish in
Regolith
Background Information:
Out of all the fruits and vegetables we considered for this experiment, we chose radish
and lion's mane. Radishes as well as Lion’s Mane are able to survive very harsh conditions such
as cold and hot weather, shortage of water, and are by nature low maintenance. We wanted to
know how radishes would grow on their own and what effect, if any, the lion’s mane will have in
the growth of radishes. There is not enough information about Lion’s Mane behavior in
symbiotic relationships such as mycorrhizae. For this reason, we decided to test our hypothesis.
Both radishes and Lion’s mane have a quick growth rate, allowing a successful
collection of data in the given 8 weeks time frame.
Nutrition wise, both organisms are excellent. Radishes are high in calcium and potassium
and also rich in antioxidants, associated with cardiovascular health and protection against free
radicals. Even though it has not been approved by the FDA, preliminary studies show that Lion’s
Mane helps with cognitive function and brain health, helps with stress, boosts mood, and
improves the skin. It’s highly nutritious and can be used as a substitute for meat.
Our hypothesis would be proven correct if the pots with radishes and Lion’s Mane grow
faster than radishes alone.

Hypothesis:
If we plant the fungi, lion's mane, together with the radish plant, the symbiotic relationship will
optimize the growth of the radish in the regolith.
Materials:
Regolith, ProMix (Potting Soil), Milogranite, Magnesium nitrate, Florikan 18 6 8, Graduated
Cylinder, Water, Thermometer, pH meter, Ferry Morse Champion Radish seeds, North Spore
Lion’s Mane Mushroom Kit.
Procedure:
1.
Prepare a mixture of soil by combining equal amounts of plain soil with ProMix. This
will be the soil used for the control group. This is Planting the Moon Mix #1
2. Prepare a mixture of 50% of the mixture prepared in step 1 with the same amount of
regolith by volume. This is Planting the Moon Mix #2. Add an equal amount of water to
both mixtures.
3. Prepare 9 pots with Planting the Moon Mix #1 and 9 Pots of Planting the Moon Mix #2.
4. Use a pH meter to measure the pH of both potting mixes and record results. Measure
moisture and record the results.
5. Place 3 radish seeds in 3 pots with Planting the Moon Mix #1 and in Planting the Moon
Mix #2.
6. Place Lion's Mane Spores in 3 pots with Planting the Moon Mix #1 and in Planting the
Moon Mix #2.
7. Place 3 radish seeds and Lion’s Mane Spores in 3 pots with Planting the Moon Mix #1
and in Planting the Moon Mix #2.
8. Place the pots in the designated area. Measure sunlight amount and record the results.
9. All the pots will be watered the same volume daily, except for the weekends. From
Tuesday to Thursday, the volume is 50mL. Mondays and Fridays, 80mL.
10. Once the seeds sprout and develop the root system, the soil amendments will be added
and plants will be replanted in bigger pots to give them the opportunity to grow further.
11. On a weekly basis, the following observations will be made for all the 18 pots. pH,
moisture (should be kept above 8), temperature, amount of sunlight, amount of leaves,
and growth in centimeters.
Soil Amendments:
On week #3 we added the soil amendments. These were the following: Milogranite, added
and mixed in all pots. Florikan 18 6 , added by mixing 5 ounces (ca. 189 gram) of product in one
gallon of water, then adding 60mL of the mixture to all the pots. Magnesium nitrate was added
Variables:
1. The presence of regolith in half of the pots. (Independent Variable) The control is regular
soil
.
2. Observable growth rate of radish plants. (Dependent variable)

3. Water, temperature, pH, amount of light, size of the pots and soil amendments. (Control
variables)

Analysis of results and conclusion:
At the beginning of this project, we theorized that by using our lion's mane/regolith mix and
taking care of the plants correctly, the results would be a successful symbiotic relationship
between radish/lion's mane. We also proposed that we would be able to see the plants grow
successfully using the regolith.
Although we planted our seeds in a shaded area in our greenhouse during the first week, the
seeds sprouted rapidly. By the third week of planting, all the plants started to develop
phototropism. In the third week, we had to replant them in bigger pots, giving the plants a
bigger space to grow. We also decided to relocate the plants to an area in which the sun was
more available, and as a result of that, they started growing rapidly. Unfortunately, between
weeks 5 and 6 most of the plants started to die except the ones with the lion's mane radish mix.
Since at the beginning the plants sprouted and grew quickly, we were able to conclude that
there must be a favorable interaction between the plant and the fungi. The fact that the small
few that were planted in the mixture of lion's mane and radish survived shows a favorable
symbiotic relationship between the fungi and plants, which can be used to maybe grow other
plants in the future.
Every experiment has its unforeseen challenges. At the start of our experiment, we placed the
plants in our school’s shaded greenhouse. Our school is currently under construction, so by the
time of the experiment, our greenhouse wasn't fully prepared. We received the regolith later so
we started planting later. Our growing period finished the week the reports were due. For the
first 3 weeks, the plants were in the shaded area of the greenhouse but we then moved them to
a place where they had sunlight throughout the day. As time went on, we noticed that the plants
were lacking water because the moisture was under 3. To improve plant health at that time we
decided to increase the amount of water being poured on the plants and we started noticing
better results.
Learning from our mistakes and difficulties, we are sure that we could have an even more
successful experiment in the future. Something that really stunted the plant growth was excess
sunlight and having a secure greenhouse from the first day. We had trouble finding a safe spot
so we had to relocate two times due to sunlight, rain, and more environmental challenges.
Maybe if there had been a secure location, we would have had better results and preparation for
the natural elements. An important thing to add is that we received the regolith later than all the
other teams, and our eighth week was this one. Leaving space for growth, having more time,
and using larger plant pots from the beginning would have prevented the process of replanting,
just to take extra caution in damaging or affecting growth. Taking responsibility and teamwork is
essential as well. Developing a good communication system in the experiment is crucial when
this amount of people are involved. Measuring correctly, checking regularly, and watering the
plants daily with extra caution and importance, will always help when doing experiments.
In conclusion, our experiment was a success, by adding lion's mane we were able to make the
regolith a good substrate for plant growth. The use of fungus to improve substrate quality can be
extrapolated to other uses in the future.
